title: October Visa Bulletin Restores EB-2 India, but Green Card Wait Still Tops 11 Years
excerpt: The State Department’s October 2026 Visa Bulletin reopens EB-2 India and moves EB-1 forward as fiscal 2027 numbers arrive — but Indian applicants still face cutoffs more than a decade behind the rest of the world.
body:
• EB-2 India is back: the final-action date is November 1, 2013, after the category went unavailable late in fiscal 2026 — but that cutoff is more than 11 years behind the January 1, 2025 date for most other countries.
  • EB-1 India moved forward more than three months to February 1, 2023; EB-3 India sits at January 1, 2014, versus May 15, 2024 for the rest of the world.
  • USCIS will accept the more generous “Dates for Filing” chart in October (EB-1: July 1, 2024; EB-2 and EB-3: January 15, 2015) — a filing window, not an approval.
  • What this means for you: if your priority date is earlier than your category’s filing cutoff, October may be your month to file Form I-485. A pending application can unlock a work permit (EAD), advance parole for international travel, and job-change portability. USCIS re-picks the chart every month, so anyone eligible and documentarily ready should speak with an immigration attorney now rather than wait.

The U.S. State Department’s October 2026 Visa Bulletin delivers a familiar mix of movement and frustration for Indian green-card applicants. As fiscal 2027’s fresh supply of immigrant visa numbers arrives, EB-2 India has been restored after going unavailable, and EB-1 India has advanced — yet the cutoffs governing Indian applicants remain more than a decade behind those for the rest of the world.

Context & Background

October marks the start of the new fiscal year, when annual immigrant-visa allocations reset. The State Department said the arrival of fiscal 2027 numbers allowed filing and final-action dates to advance across several categories. The worldwide employment-based preference level is at least 140,000 visas a year, but the roughly 7% per-country limit is the bottleneck: India is one of four oversubscribed countries, and its large pipeline exhausts its share quickly.

EB-2 India’s absence is recent. On May 22, 2026, the State Department announced that all EB-2 immigrant visas for India had been used for fiscal 2026, and the category went unavailable for the remainder of the year. Its return at November 1, 2013 is about eight months behind where it sat (around July 15, 2014) before the pause — a typical conservative early-year reset.

This follows a grim drumbeat: our August coverage documented a backlog trapping nearly one million Indians, with the EB-2 wait projected at 179 years, and the August and September bulletins warned repeatedly that Indian EB-1 numbers could run out.

Impact & Analysis

The numbers tell two stories. Final-action dates — the ones that determine when a green card can actually be approved — show the depth of the backlog: EB-2 India at November 1, 2013 versus January 1, 2025 for most countries; EB-3 India at January 1, 2014 versus May 15, 2024; EB-1 India at February 1, 2023, up from October 15, 2022.

The second story is the filing chart. Each month, USCIS decides whether adjustment-of-status applicants may use the more generous “Dates for Filing” chart. For October it chose the filing chart — after using the restrictive Final Action chart every month from May through September. That matters: an Indian EB-2 or EB-3 applicant with a priority date before January 15, 2015, or an EB-1 applicant before July 1, 2024, may now file Form I-485.

Filing is not approval — but it is consequential. A pending I-485 can allow an applicant to seek an employment authorization document and advance parole, give H-4 and other dependents more flexibility, and provide protections if a job changes under portability rules. Immigration attorneys describe it as a filing opportunity, not a visa number; one practitioner called October a significant reset for Indian employment-based immigration, not a broad-based breakthrough in the backlog.

Diaspora Angle

For the hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals who have spent their careers on H-1B status while waiting out the queue, October’s bulletin is the rare piece of constructive news in an otherwise bruising year — one dominated by the $100,000 H-1B fee fight, the proposed end of the 60-day grace period for laid-off workers, and a proposed $70,000-per-student OPT fee. The backlog’s structure hasn’t changed, but for applicants with 2014–era priority dates, a filing window is a tangible step out of limbo: work authorization independent of an employer, and the ability to travel without jeopardizing a pending case.

What’s Next

Whether November keeps the filing chart is unknown — USCIS reassesses monthly. The State Department has also warned that some worldwide employment-based categories retrogressed in October despite the new fiscal-year numbers, and demand will be monitored with dates adjusted as needed. Visa Bulletin dates remain an allocation mechanism, not a timetable: they can move forward, stall, or move backward. For anyone eligible this month, the practical advice from practitioners is consistent — if you are documentarily ready, file in October rather than gamble on November.
